title: Short Stuff: The Pledge of Allegiance
summary: Short Stuff episode on the history of the Pledge of Allegiance. Josh and Chuck recount how the pledge was written by Francis Bellamy, a Christian socialist and assistant editor at The Youth Companion magazine, as a patriotic program for schools tied to the 1892 Columbian Exposition in Chicago (World's Fair) and the Columbus anniversary. They cover the earlier 1885 pledge by George T. Balch, Bellamy's wording and the dropped "liberty, equality, fraternity" idea, the Bellamy salute and its resemblance to the later Nazi salute, the 1923 change from "my flag" to "the flag of the United States" and the addition of "of America", New York becoming the first state to make pledge recitation compulsory in schools, the 1954 addition of "under God" at the Knights of Columbus and Eisenhower's urging, and the Supreme Court decision West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette that students cannot be forced to recite it.

segments.title: Opening and recitation of the pledge
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode by reciting the Pledge of Allegiance from memory, joking about how they got the words wrong, and introduce the pledge as a marketing tool for a magazine.

segments.title: Francis Bellamy and the Youth Companion
segments.summary: The hosts describe Francis Bellamy, an assistant editor at The Youth Companion, and his cousin Edward Bellamy, author of the utopian novel Looking Backward. Francis was a Christian socialist who wanted immigrants Americanized, especially through public schools.

segments.title: Columbian Exposition and the schools program
segments.summary: The Youth Companion planned a patriotic program for schools tied to the 1892 Columbian Exposition in Chicago and the Columbus anniversary, to boost patriotism and subscriptions and sell flags. Bellamy was assigned to write the material.

segments.title: Earlier pledge, Bellamy's wording, and the salute
segments.summary: George T. Balch wrote an earlier pledge in 1885 for Flag Day. Bellamy found it childish and wrote his own version, which was recited in schools. He also proposed a salute that resembled the later Nazi salute, though it predated the Nazis.

segments.title: Wording changes and compulsory recitation
segments.summary: In 1923 the National Flag Conference changed 'my flag' to 'the flag of the United States' and then 'of America' was added. New York became the first state to make pledge recitation compulsory in schools, and more states followed around World War One.

segments.title: Under God and the Supreme Court
segments.summary: The phrase 'under God' was added at the urging of the Knights of Columbus and Eisenhower, who said schools faced threat from godless communists. Students were compelled to recite until the Supreme Court's West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette decision said no one can be forced to say it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank a producer, note the article is posted on the HowStuffWorks website, and sign off.
